title: Valid Sudoku
pattern: hash set membership / grid constraint tracking
statement:
A partially filled Sudoku board arrives as a grid of integers with R rows and C columns. A cell holding 0 is empty, any other cell holds a clue digit from 1 to 9. Draw the grid lines every three rows and every three columns: on the classic 9 x 9 board those lines cut exactly nine 3 x 3 boxes, and on any other grid they cut the same 3 x 3 tiles with the last row or column of tiles left partial. A position is legal when no digit appears twice inside one row, twice inside one column, or twice inside one of those boxes.

Decide whether the given position is legal. The board does not have to be completable and does not have to be full: an all-zero board is legal, and repeating a digit is legal as long as the repeats never share a row, a column or a box.

Return true when the position is legal and false otherwise.

Constraints: `1 <= board.length <= 200` and `1 <= board[i].length <= 200` and `0 <= board[i][j] <= 9`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: The straightforward check costs one full scan of a cell's row, column and box per clue; that already answers the question, just slowly.
Instead of rescanning, keep one set per row, one per column and one per box, and test membership before inserting the clue.

The box of cell (r, c) is (r / 3) * boxColumns + (c / 3) using integer division, where boxColumns is the number of 3-wide column tiles in the grid, and 0 must be skipped before anything touches a set.

editorial.approach: The brute force treats every clue as a question it answers by rescanning: for each filled cell it walks the other cells of its row, the other cells of its column, and the cells of the 3 x 3 box the grid lines cut around it, so a single clue costs O(max(R, C)) and the whole board costs O(R * C * max(R, C)) with R rows and C columns. It never stores anything, which is why its space is O(1). The optimal keeps one hash set per row, one per column and one per box, and asks each set a membership question before inserting: a clue that a set already holds makes the position illegal. On the classic 9 x 9 board that is 27 sets and 81 lookups for the whole scan.
editorial.why_optimal: Every cell has to be read at least once, so O(R * C) is the floor and the single pass reaches it. Each set holds at most one entry per distinct clue per constraint, so 9 entries each, which is O(R * C) overall but only 81 labels on a 9 x 9 board. With R = C = 9 the win is not asymptotic noise but real work removed: the rescanning version performs 27 comparisons per clue, close to 2000 comparisons for a dense board, against 81 lookups.
editorial.pitfalls: Forgetting that 0 is not a clue, so every empty cell collides with every other empty cell and legal boards are rejected. Computing the box index as (r / 3) * boxColumns + (c / 3) but with float division or with the wrong pairing, which silently merges boxes and hides real conflicts. Hard-coding boxColumns as 3, or dropping it entirely, which happens to be right on a 9 x 9 board and quietly merges or splits boxes on any other width. Walking a fixed 3 x 3 block of cells around the current one without clamping it to the grid, which reads a row that does not exist: a crash in Python and an undefined comparison in JavaScript. Reading board[r][c] once into a variable and then comparing the variable against itself, which misses duplicates. Mutating the board to mark seen digits, which corrupts the caller's input.
